EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

Add your team’s context

The harness behaves correctly only if it can see your team’s business domain, standards, policies and conventions at the right moment. This page shows where each kind of context enters the PO/BA and developer harnesses, and how to add your own.

This page is for Tech Leads and the people who own a team’s standards and policies. For how to structure instructions so a session loads only what it needs, read Layer instructions and context. Exact file names, registry entries and environment settings are in the harness repository.

Know what context each stage needs

Feed in each kind of context at the stage where it shapes a decision. Loading it earlier dilutes the agent’s attention; loading it later means the decision has already been made without it.

Context to add at each stage, the skills that use it and why it matters
StageContextUsed byWhy it matters
1. Requirements and scopeBusiness domain intent, persona maps, scope boundaries/speckit.specify, /wayfinder, CLARAGrounds the user stories in the business problem, so the team does not build the wrong features.
2. Architecture and designShared architecture standards, integration recipes, ADR templates/dependency-orchestrator, /wayfinderApplies structural constraints, such as authentication, logging and database schema, before work is sliced, so design flaws do not spread into every issue.
3. Compliance and governanceRegulatory and security policies, such as IM8 and ARC/spec-complianceAudits the TRD against policy, so security controls are declared and resolved before coding.
4. ImplementationCoding practices, framework guides, API reference documentation/do-work, through /query-kbGives the agent syntax, language features and library patterns, so code passes type checks, builds and tests.
5. Merge reviewRepository style, conventions and lint expectations/code-review, with CODING_STANDARDS.mdKeeps changes consistent with the team’s style, naming rules and codebase conventions before merging.

Source: [1] context ingestion matrix.

Add business domain context

During requirements, the business domain enters through the specification files that the PO or BA commits. How you supply it depends on the PO/BA path:

  • Path 1, SpecKit: supply your domain context, terminology glossaries or functional requirements in the prompt or as reference files when you run /speckit.specify, so spec.md uses your team’s vocabulary.
  • Path 2, Socratic workflow: reference your domain models, legacy codebase patterns or business-logic guides when you run /wayfinder. Use /domain-modeling and /codebase-design to keep tickets and ADRs in your team’s ubiquitous language.
  • Path 3, CLARA: upload your domain documentation to the Confluence spaces or knowledge bases that CLARA queries, so personas, journey maps and specifications in specs/ reflect your business.

Whichever path you use, the committed specification files carry the domain context into the developer harness as the source-of-truth handoff.

Source: [1] section 1.

Add shared standards and recipes

During planning, the harness matches each story to implementation standards. The base library is AppStandards, cloned from the shared repository or from a team fork.

AppStandards uses the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), which stores documentation as a version-controlled graph of Markdown concepts. This lets the agent load only what a story needs:

  • Catalogue entry points: each folder has an index.md listing its concepts, so the agent can find a guideline without scanning the whole tree.
  • Concept files: each standard is split into focused files with strict rules, code recipes, and questions for challenging or verifying a design.
  • Story-to-standard mapping: /dependency-orchestrator (Step 2) maps each user story to its specific sub-standards, such as core MFA or single sign-on. /wayfinder (Step 5) and /do-work (Step 12) then read only those few files, instead of the whole catalogue, which would exceed the context window and dilute attention.

To add your own standards:

  1. Follow the OKF layout. Structure your standards folder with index.md catalogues, rule documents, code recipes and challenge questions.
  2. Register them with the orchestrator. Add your standards’ locations to the dependency orchestrator’s standards registry, so it can map stories to them.
  3. Tag your stories. Tag task nodes in your stories or foundation templates with your standard’s key. The orchestrator then lists the standard in the Developer Delivery Plan.

Sources: [1] section 2; [2] section 2.1, Step 2.

Add coding practices to the knowledge base

During implementation, the agent retrieves coding practices and framework patterns from your organisation’s hosted Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Inside the /do-work loop (Step 12), the implementer calls /query-kb, which routes each file to a query category, such as a TSX file to a React query.

To add your own context, upload your design guides, library documentation and coding conventions to the data source synced to your team’s knowledge base, then run a sync. Point /query-kb at your knowledge base by its ID or by a tag; the skills catalogue lists the flags.

Sources: [1] section 3; [3] Additional skills.

Add security and governance policies

Before work is sliced into issues, /spec-compliance (Step 8) audits the TRD against the policy references held by the policies skill and writes a checklist report. Two references ship with the harness:

  • IM8: 36 application security controls from Instruction Manual 8.
  • ARC: 88 agentic AI governance controls from the Agentic Risk & Capability Framework.

To enforce your own policies, write your compliance checklist or internal security policy as a Markdown file, add it to the policies skill’s references, and register it in that skill. The policy reviewer then applies it alongside IM8 and ARC.

Sources: [1] section 4; [3] Compliance skills.

Add review rules

At the end of the development loop, changes are checked against the repository’s own conventions. Put them in CODING_STANDARDS.md at the root of the application repository: formatting rules, naming, design principles and lint-like expectations.

/code-review (Step 15, and inside Gate 2 of /do-work) checks the diff against this file in a parallel sub-agent. Where the file is silent, it falls back to a baseline of common code smells.

Sources: [1] section 5; [2] section 2.5.

Set up your team’s context

A new project team can work through this checklist once. When it is complete, every stage in the table above has the context it needs.

  1. Write local coding rules. Create or edit CODING_STANDARDS.md at the repository root with your naming, architecture patterns and formatting expectations.
  2. Configure the knowledge base. Upload your coding standards, library documentation and technical guidelines to your team’s Bedrock data source, run a sync, and configure your environment so /query-kb targets it.
  3. Connect your architecture standards. Clone your standards repository in the OKF layout, register it with the orchestrator and tag your stories with its keys.
  4. Define security policies. Write any additional corporate security policies as Markdown, add them to the policies skill and register them.
  5. Declare architecture boundary tests. Run /arch-tests-plan (Step 4) to scan the project and produce arch/arch-test-plan.md. Review the rules, customise them if you have your own layering or dependency restrictions, then run /arch-tests-gen.

Next step: complete items 1 and 5 first, because they need only the repository. Then take your first story through planning and note which context the agent asked for but could not find.

Source: [1] quick-start checklist.
